summary: Specifies Datagram Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery, a robust way for a datagram transport or application to discover whether a network path supports a given datagram size. It does this by probing, without relying only on ICMP messages. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A datagram sender has to guess how large a packet the network will carry. This RFC says to test that by sending probe packets of a chosen size and waiting to see whether the far end confirms receiving them, instead of relying on error messages that may never arrive.

subtitle: How a datagram sender finds the largest packet a path will carry, by sending probes instead of waiting for error messages.

tldr.problem: A datagram sender has to know the largest packet a network path will carry. The usual method depends on ICMP Packet Too Big messages that are often rate limited, filtered by firewalls, lost in tunnels or impossible to validate, so oversized packets are silently discarded.
tldr.mechanism: The sender sends probe packets of a chosen size and treats an acknowledgment from the far end as proof that the size works. A state machine with timers raises the size when probes succeed and drops back to a smaller size when they stop arriving.
tldr.outcome: Datagram transports and applications get a way to find and track the usable packet size without depending on ICMP. It updates RFC 4821, RFC 4960, RFC 6951, RFC 8085 and RFC 8261 so that they point to this method.

facts.label: PROBE_TIMER minimum
facts.value: 1 second, and larger than 15 seconds is recommended

today: RFC 8899 is a Proposed Standard from September 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4821, RFC 4960, RFC 6951, RFC 8085 and RFC 8261 so that they point to this method.

sections.title: Why Classical Path MTU Discovery Breaks
sections.content:
Path MTU Discovery finds the largest packet that can travel across a network path without being split up. The classical method, described in RFC 1191 and RFC 8201, relies on the network sending back an ICMP message when a packet is too large. This document calls both the IPv4 ICMP Unreachable message carrying the error Fragmentation Needed (Type 3, Code 4) and the ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message (Type 2) a PTB message. When a sender receives one it lowers the effective MTU to the value reported in it, and it periodically sends larger probe packets to find out whether the path can carry more.

The RFC lists the ways in which that error message never arrives. The generation of ICMP messages is usually rate limited. Firewalls can filter ICMP. When a router drops a packet inside a tunnel, the message goes to the tunnel ingress, which has to rewrite it and forward it, and a failure there stops it reaching the sender. Asymmetric forwarding, policy-based or Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) routing, or a middlebox acting as an application load balancer can leave no return route to the sender. A packet can also be dropped by a misconfigured layer 2 switch or a misconfigured Maximum Receive Unit (MRU), in which case no error message is generated at all. The result is a black hole: every datagram larger than the real path MTU is discarded and the sender is not told.

Even a message that does arrive may be impossible to check. A router that implements RFC 792 is only required to quote the first 64 bits of the IP payload, which may leave too little to identify the flow. Tunnels and encryption shrink the quoted packet further. A NAT device that translates packet headers should also translate the quoted packet inside the ICMP message, and if it does not, the sender cannot match the message to the flow that caused it. A node that is not on the path can also send a forged PTB message to push a sender's effective MTU down.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual way to find the largest usable packet size depends on an error message coming back from the network. This RFC lists the ways that message goes missing, and then defines a method that works by sending test packets instead.

sections.title: What a Datagram Transport Must Provide
sections.content:
Section 3 lists nine requirements for a datagram PL. The ones that shape the design are these.

  • Managing the PLPMTU: a PL MUST NOT send a datagram other than a probe packet that is larger than the current PLPMTU.
  • Probe packets: the interface below the PL must be able to send a probe larger than the PLPMTU. In IPv4 the probe MUST carry the Don't Fragment (DF) bit; in IPv6 a probe is always sent without source fragmentation.
  • Reception feedback: the destination PL must be able to tell the sender that a probe arrived.
  • Probe loss recovery: probes that carry no user data are RECOMMENDED, so a lost probe needs no retransmission. If a probe does carry data that would need retransmission, the PL or the layers above it must arrange that retransmission.
  • PMTU parameters: a sender is RECOMMENDED to use what it knows about the local link MTU, and may use what the receiver reports about the size it can accept.
  • Processing PTB messages: a received PTB message MUST be validated before use, and it MUST NOT be used to raise the PLPMTU.
  • Probing and congestion control: where probes are not paced by a congestion controller, the interval between them MUST be at least one RTT, and the loss of a probe SHOULD NOT be treated as congestion.
  • Probing and flow control: flow control SHOULD NOT apply to the PLPMTU when probes carry no user data.
  • Shared PLPMTU state: the value may also be stored with the destination entry in the IP layer cache, so that other PL instances sharing the path can use it.

Further principles require the method to survive path changes, reordering, delay and duplication, and to tell the application how much data fits in one datagram without forcing an unnecessarily small size while the search is still running.
sections.plainLanguage: A datagram transport has to provide three things before this method works: it must be able to send a test packet larger than the size it is currently using, the far end must confirm receipt of that packet, and it must never send ordinary data larger than the size it has proved.

sections.title: Probes, Black Holes and the Maximum Packet Size
sections.content:
A probe packet is a datagram sent with a purposely chosen size, normally the current PLPMTU or larger, to find out whether a packet of that size reaches the far end. A datagram PL builds one in one of three ways: control information together with padding, an application data block together with padding, or an application data block of exactly the right size. The receiver must be able to tell the added padding from the real data, so that padding is never passed to the application. The size of a probe includes every header and every byte of padding added to it, including security fields such as an AEAD tag and TLS record layer padding. Each probe must carry enough information to identify it uniquely within the Maximum Segment Lifetime, which this document takes as 2 minutes.

Confirmation of a probe depends on the transport. SCTP, DCCP and QUIC can report that they received a specific datagram, and that report can acknowledge the probe. UDP and UDP-Lite have no such mechanism, so an application protocol has to provide one.

Black hole detection has three possible indicators: a validated PTB message reporting a size below the current PLPMTU, which the method MUST NOT rely on alone; repeated loss of probes at the current size, tracked by the PROBE_COUNT counter; or an event from the transport showing excessive loss at one packet size. When a black hole is detected, the method sets a lower PLPMTU and a lower MPS, and then confirms that the new size works.

The Maximum Packet Size (MPS) is the largest block of application data that fits in one datagram. It is the PLPMTU minus the PL headers and their overhead, including security overhead. A PL should offer a primitive that returns the current MPS to the application. A PL implementing this specification MUST suspend the network layer's own PMTU enforcement for each flow that uses it, and use the size this method produces instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe packet is a datagram padded to an exact size. The far end confirms it, and that confirmation is the proof that the size works. The maximum packet size is what is left for the application once the transport and IP headers are subtracted.

sections.title: Responding to Packet Too Big Messages
sections.content:
PTB messages are optional hints. A simple implementation may ignore them entirely, in which case the PLPMTU does not change when one arrives. A transport that does use them must validate each one first, by checking that the IP addresses, the protocol and the source and destination ports in the quoted packet match traffic the endpoint actually sent, and by using information that an off-path attacker cannot easily guess, such as a value known only to the two endpoints. A message that fails validation must not be used at all.

A validated message reports a next-hop link MTU, called PTB_SIZE. Before it can be used, the headers below the packetization layer are subtracted to give PL_PTB_SIZE. A validated message may speed up the search by prompting an immediate probe of that size, but it MUST NOT set the PLPMTU directly. The RFC sorts the reported size into five cases. Below MIN_PLPMTU it is invalid and the message is discarded without further processing. Between MIN_PLPMTU and BASE_PLPMTU it may mean the path cannot sustain the base size, and a robust implementation may enter the ERROR state, with a threshold of 68 bytes for IPv4 and 1280 bytes for IPv6. Between BASE_PLPMTU and the current PLPMTU it may indicate a black hole, in which case the PLPMTU is set back to BASE_PLPMTU and a new search starts, using the reported size as its starting point. Between the PLPMTU and the PROBED_SIZE the current PLPMTU stays valid, and the reported size can be used as the next point to search. At or above the PROBED_SIZE the signal is inconsistent, and the message is discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A too-big error message is only a hint. The sender must check that the message refers to a packet it actually sent, and it may use the reported size to choose the next test size, but it may not set the working size from the message alone.

sections.title: Timers, Constants and Variables
sections.content:
The method uses up to three timers. The PROBE_TIMER bounds how long the sender waits for the acknowledgment of a probe; it MUST NOT be smaller than 1 second and SHOULD be larger than 15 seconds. The PMTU_RAISE_TIMER has a period of 600 seconds, after which the sender returns to the search phase to look for a larger size. The CONFIRMATION_TIMER is the period a sender waits before re-checking the current size, and it MUST NOT be used with a transport that acknowledges data, such as SCTP.

Four constants bound the search. MAX_PROBES is the limit on consecutive failed probes of any size, with a default value of 3; a value greater than 1 gives robustness against isolated packet loss. MIN_PLPMTU is the smallest size the method will attempt: for IPv6 it must be at least the size that results in a 1280-byte IPv6 packet, and for IPv4 it must be at least the size that results in a 68-byte IPv4 packet. MAX_PLPMTU is the largest size the method will attempt, bounded by the outgoing interface MTU and, when known, by the size the remote endpoint can receive. BASE_PLPMTU is a configured size expected to work on most paths; for most PLs a suitable value is larger than 1200 bytes, and for IPv4 a default of 1200 bytes is RECOMMENDED.

Two variables track progress. PROBED_SIZE is the size of the probe in flight, a tentative value waiting for confirmation. PROBE_COUNT counts successive probes that were not acknowledged, and it returns to zero whenever a probe is acknowledged.
sections.plainLanguage: The method uses up to three timers, four constants and two counters. The timers say how long to wait for an answer and how often to look for a larger size; the counters record how many probes have failed in a row.

sections.title: The Five States
sections.content:
The method runs a state machine for each path; a sender that supports multipath or multihoming needs one per path. DISABLED is the initial state and is entered again whenever the transport reports a loss of connectivity. BASE confirms that the BASE_PLPMTU size is supported: on entry the PROBED_SIZE is set to BASE_PLPMTU and the PROBE_COUNT to zero, and each probe starts the PROBE_TIMER. SEARCHING is the main probing state. Each acknowledged probe sets the PROBE_COUNT to zero, raises the PLPMTU to the PROBED_SIZE, and the search algorithm then chooses a larger size to try. SEARCH_COMPLETE is the normal maintenance state, where the PL is not probing to raise the PLPMTU. ERROR covers a path that is not known to support even the BASE_PLPMTU size, or one that produces contradictory information, and it exists to stop the MPS offered to the higher layer from oscillating.

SEARCHING ends when the PROBE_COUNT reaches MAX_PROBES, when a validated PTB message reports a size equal to the last one that worked, or when a probe of size MAX_PLPMTU is acknowledged. A black hole detected in SEARCHING sends the sender back to BASE. In SEARCH_COMPLETE the PMTU_RAISE_TIMER eventually returns the sender to SEARCHING to look for a larger size. For a transport that does not acknowledge data, the CONFIRMATION_TIMER periodically schedules a probe at the current PLPMTU, and if MAX_PROBES of those fail the method returns to BASE. The ERROR state is left, and SEARCHING entered, once the path is consistent again and the BASE_PLPMTU has been confirmed.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender moves through five states. It first proves that a basic size works, then searches for a larger one, then keeps the best size it found. If probes stop arriving it falls back to the basic size, and if the path gives contradictory information it waits in an error state.

sections.title: Applying the Method to UDP, SCTP and QUIC
sections.content:
The method needs protocol-specific details, and the RFC supplies them for the transports it names. UDP and UDP-Lite do not provide what is needed, so an application using them implements the method itself, with an application-layer request and response to confirm a probe. The response should carry a value known only to the two endpoints, such as a session ID or an initialised sequence number, and an application should not run the method when the transport underneath already provides it. An application with no other way to confirm connectivity should use acknowledged probes before entering the BASE state, and one with no other way to confirm correct delivery should run the CONFIRMATION_TIMER while in the SEARCH_COMPLETE state.

For SCTP the recommended probe is a PAD chunk, as defined in RFC 4820, attached to a minimum-length HEARTBEAT chunk. The HEARTBEAT ACK confirms the probe, and this keeps probing clear of user messages, congestion control and flow control. Because SCTP acknowledges data, it must not use the CONFIRMATION_TIMER. For SCTP over UDP the probe size includes the 8 bytes of the UDP header, and for SCTP over DTLS the DTLS headers reduce the payload available for padding. The RFC notes that neither RFC 4960 nor this document gives a way to validate the ICMP payload for SCTP over DTLS, which can prevent PTB messages being processed there.

QUIC is a UDP-based transport that provides reception feedback, so from the point of view of this method it can act as an acknowledged transport, and the QUIC specification describes how it uses the method.
sections.plainLanguage: Each transport needs its own way to build a test packet of an exact size and confirm it. The RFC gives one for applications over UDP, one for SCTP and its UDP and DTLS forms, and points at the QUIC specification for QUIC itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concern is a PTB message that has been forged or that reports the wrong size. A node supporting this method must validate the payload of a PTB message so that it can tell the message was sent in response to traffic it really sent. An on-path attacker can still produce a PTB message with a valid quoted packet and drive the PLPMTU down. Two mitigations are given: the sender never reduces the PLPMTU below the base size on the strength of a PTB message alone, because it first enters the BASE state; and the design does not require PTB processing, so a sender can suspend it.

Other points from the RFC: the interval between individual probes must be at least one RTT, and the interval between rounds of probing is set by the PMTU_RAISE_TIMER. The mechanism that confirms receipt of a probe must resist off-path injection, which protocols such as TCP and SCTP do with a randomly initialised sequence number. Parsing the quoted packet inside a PTB message adds work per packet and should be limited, because arbitrary headers could be used for a denial-of-service attack; rate-limiting that work may cause PTB messages to be missed, which the method tolerates. Probing may add padding to a datagram, and where the transport uses cryptographic confidentiality or integrity the design should not add anything that those mechanisms do not cover. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is a forged too-big message that makes the sender shrink its packets. The rules require the sender to check the message against traffic it really sent, to never go below the basic size because of a message alone, and to be able to ignore these messages entirely.

items.title: PROBE_TIMER
items.text: How long the sender waits for a probe acknowledgment. Not smaller than 1 second, and larger than 15 seconds is recommended.

items.title: PMTU_RAISE_TIMER
items.text: 600 seconds. When it expires the sender starts searching for a larger size again.

items.title: CONFIRMATION_TIMER
items.text: How often an unacknowledged transport re-checks the current size. Not used with an acknowledged transport such as SCTP.

items.title: MAX_PROBES
items.text: The limit on consecutive failed probes of any size. The default value is 3.

items.title: MIN_PLPMTU
items.text: The smallest size tried: at least the size that gives a 1280-byte IPv6 packet or a 68-byte IPv4 packet.

items.title: MAX_PLPMTU
items.text: The largest size tried, bounded by the outgoing interface MTU and by what the far end can receive.

items.title: BASE_PLPMTU
items.text: A size expected to work on most paths. For IPv4 a default of 1200 bytes is recommended.

items.title: PROBE_COUNT
items.text: Counts probes that were not acknowledged. It returns to zero as soon as one probe is acknowledged.
